title: What to Eat in Guadalajara: Tortas Ahogadas, Birria and a First Food Day
dek: Three distinctive dishes, one unhurried food day. Use this short list to choose a meal worth making time for, then fit it around the neighborhood you are already exploring.
body:
First trip at a glance

  • Start with: Torta ahogada
  • Slow down for: Birria
  • Another classic: Carne en su jugo
  • Leave room: Jericalla

Choose your first dish

A torta ahogada is a pork-filled birote sandwich covered in tomato and chile sauces. Tortas Toño is one option listed by Jalisco tourism. Ask about the heat before ordering; a sauce-drenched sandwich is a sit-down pause, not a practical walking snack.

Birria is a chile-and-spice meat preparation, traditionally goat and also made with beef. Birriería Las 9 Esquinas is another tourism-listed starting point. Confirm the meat and preparation rather than assuming every birria is the same.

A second meal with a different character

Carne en su jugo combines beef, broth, beans and bacon; Kamilos 333 is a listed place to try it. For dessert, look for jericalla, the local baked milk-and-egg sweet.

Those dish descriptions and restaurant suggestions come from Jalisco tourism’s food guide. This is a researched shortlist, rather than a claim that we have eaten at every table.

How to turn the list into a day

Pick one substantial lunch, then leave your next meal open. Trying the torta, birria and beef dish back-to-back would turn a useful tasting plan into an endurance test. For two days, spread them across separate lunches or dinners.

Build the rest of the day around Colonia Americana or the historic center. Check your chosen restaurant’s actual branch on a map before linking it to sightseeing; this list is not a promised walking route.

Before you choose a table

Ask about meat, dairy and sauces if you have dietary requirements. Look at the menu and total before ordering, and use the venue’s own page to confirm service on your travel date. If you book a food tour, compare the number of tastings and what is included with what you actually want to try.

title: Antigua Guatemala Breakfast and Coffee: Fernando’s Kaffee or Café Condesa?
dek: Choose a café with a reason to be there, then leave room for courtyards, cobblestones and an unhurried lunch.
body:
Your food plan at a glance

  • Breakfast option: Fernando’s Kaffee
  • Another café stop: Café Condesa
  • Best approach: One main stop per morning
  • Check directly: Menus and dietary needs

Fernando’s Kaffee: start with breakfast in mind

Fernando’s Kaffee describes itself as a coffee roastery, café and restaurant. Its menu page highlights a desayuno típico and sweet crêpes with chocolate and pepitoria spread. Those details give you a concrete reason to consider it if you want a breakfast-led start, rather than simply another coffee on the way somewhere else.

Read the current menu before choosing what to order. If breakfast will be the main meal of your morning, leave room to enjoy it. If you only want coffee, keep lunch as a separate decision instead of assuming a café visit will cover it.

Café Condesa: a second option to compare

Café Condesa describes a central setting and food prepared on site; its own history dates its Antigua presence to 1993. Add it to your shortlist when you want a sit-down café stop, and look at its current offering before deciding whether that means breakfast, lunch or coffee with something small.

Compare the two cafés against your actual route. You can spread them over two mornings, choose just one, or return to the place you enjoyed. A useful itinerary leaves space for a favorite instead of requiring a new venue at every meal.

Make lunch a separate decision

Before heading out, decide whether lunch is likely to be a substantial break or a lighter stop. Use current menus to make that choice. A label such as café or restaurant is less helpful than knowing whether the available food suits your group that day.

Ask directly about dietary requirements, ingredients and preparation when those matter. This shortlist does not establish allergen handling, substitutions or current availability. It also avoids quoting prices and opening hours that can change between planning and arrival.

A simple two-morning plan

  • First morning: choose one café for breakfast, then continue with your city walk.
  • First afternoon: choose lunch around your location and appetite, rather than a rigid food checklist.
  • Second morning: try the other café if it fits, or return to your favorite.
  • Keep a special dinner separate from an already full afternoon of eating.

Use our three-day Antigua itinerary to connect meals with the rest of your stay. The Antigua first-timer’s guide covers the broader destination; choose the sightseeing first, then place the café stop where it makes the day easier.

For a short visit, fewer commitments often make a better plan. Save the cafés, check their current service details before you go, and keep a backup in mind if your first choice does not work that day.

title: Where to Eat in Old San Juan: Coffee, Puerto Rican Lunch and a Chocolate Stop
dek: A short, useful food shortlist for the historic district—with time left for the streets between the tables.
body:
Your food plan at a glance

  • Start with: Puerto Rican coffee
  • Lunch focus: Puerto Rican cooking
  • Plan around: Your old-city sightseeing
  • Before you go: Check current menus and service

Coffee at Café Don Ruiz

Start by choosing the part of Old San Juan you want to explore, then put coffee along that route. Discover Puerto Rico’s coffee guide includes Café Don Ruiz inside the Cuartel de Ballajá and notes its family coffee-roasting tradition. If that building is already on your sightseeing shortlist, the café is a useful option to investigate.

Keep this a pause rather than a second breakfast appointment. Have a look at the current offering, decide whether you want something to eat, and leave your lunch plans flexible. A coffee stop is also a good moment to check the route to your next sight.

Café Manolín for a Puerto Rican lunch

The tourism board describes Café Manolín as a small Old San Juan restaurant specializing in Puerto Rican food. Put it on your shortlist when you want lunch in the same district as your sightseeing, rather than traveling elsewhere just for a meal.

Review the current menu before settling on it. This is a cuisine-led recommendation, not a promise of a particular dish, price or opening time. If someone in your group has a dietary requirement, ask the restaurant about the actual preparation rather than relying on a broad cuisine label.

Two alternatives with a specific reason to visit

Discover Puerto Rico’s San Juan guide highlights Princesa Gastrobar for mofongo and Chocobar Cortés for its use of chocolate in dishes. These give you two different directions for the same food stop: investigate Princesa if mofongo is on your list, or look at Chocobar’s menu if the chocolate angle appeals.

Choose one based on the menu, your appetite and the rest of the day. Treat them as alternatives, rather than trying to fit every restaurant into one afternoon. Confirm the current location and service details before making a special detour.

How to fit the food into your day

  • Choose one coffee stop close to the sights you already want to visit.
  • Save a lunch choice and one backup, with the current menu links.
  • Allow time to sit down; avoid placing a meal immediately before a timed attraction.
  • If you are heading back to Condado or another neighborhood, account for that journey before making an evening reservation.

Start with our San Juan first-timer’s guide for the wider city plan. Still choosing your base? Compare Old San Juan, Condado and Ocean Park before committing to a food itinerary centered on one neighborhood.

title: Oaxaca’s Central Markets: Benito Juárez and 20 de Noviembre for First-Timers
dek: Browse first, arrive hungry, and leave room for conversation: a practical introduction to two of Oaxaca’s central markets.
body:
At a Glance

  • Browse and shop: Benito Juárez
  • Meal-led stop: 20 de Noviembre
  • Best approach: A flexible market morning
  • Before ordering: Ask what is included

Two markets, one relaxed plan

Oaxaca’s central markets deserve more than a quick photo stop between reservations. For a first visit, pair browsing at Benito Juárez with time for a meal at 20 de Noviembre. This is our suggested sequence, not a fixed route or a claim that every stall keeps the same hours.

Use the Oaxaca destination hub for the wider stay, and read our Oaxaca culture and boutique-living guide before shaping the day. Leave yourself enough flexibility to pause when something interests you, rather than arriving with a checklist of everything you must buy or eat.

Benito Juárez: look before you choose

The official Benito Juárez market guide describes a central market selling food, clothing, crafts and everyday goods. Its range includes regional snacks and drinks, cheeses, dried chiles and mezcal, alongside items that serve daily local life.

Take an initial look around before making purchases. Ask what a product is, who made it and how to care for or store it. With crafts, ask about materials and origin instead of assuming every piece has the same story. With food to take home, check the rules for your destination before buying anything you may be unable to carry across a border.

20 de Noviembre: give lunch room

Oaxaca Tourism’s 20 de Noviembre overview highlights the market’s traditional cooking and its well-known grill corridor, where tasajo, cecina and chorizo are among the foods described. Chocolate, mole and other regional flavors also belong to the wider market story.

Choose a meal because it appeals to you, not because you feel obliged to order everything. Before committing, ask how the portion is priced, what comes with it and which accompaniments cost extra. If ingredients matter to you, ask the vendor directly rather than guessing from the name or appearance of a dish.

A simple morning that leaves room for discovery

  1. Begin with a browse: get oriented and note what you might return for.
  2. Choose one meal or tasting priority: leave the rest as possibilities.
  3. Make considered purchases: ask questions and keep track of what you can carry comfortably.
  4. Keep the afternoon flexible: return to the Centro, pause at your accommodation or continue exploring only if you want to.

For help with context and ordering, a food walk can be useful. Compare the guide’s itinerary, group size, meeting point and included tastings; do not assume that “market tour” means every sample or meal is included.

Shop and photograph with care

These are working markets. Leave space for customers and deliveries, ask before photographing people or their stalls, and make room for a seller to finish serving someone else. A small bag that closes and leaves your hands free is more useful here than bringing everything you packed for the trip.

If your interests extend to craft communities, read our Chiapas and Oaxaca cultural-immersion story. Treat a workshop visit as a separate outing with its own arrangements, not something to tack onto lunch without checking the journey and access.

Build the rest of the Oaxaca stay

Balance this food-led day with a different kind of experience. The Sierra Norte mountain-biking guide introduces an outdoor option; compare the physical demands and local arrangements before choosing it. For a wider food itinerary, browse Latin America for food and wine lovers.

Use the Jet Set trip planner to keep separate outings realistic, then return to the Oaxaca hub for the neighborhood and stay overview. If the journey continues, the Mexico City and Guadalajara hubs are useful next starting points.

title: Where to Stay in Medellín: El Poblado or Laureles?
dek: Two popular bases, two different rhythms. Choose the part of Medellín that fits your mornings and evenings.
body:
At a Glance

  • Restaurants and nightlife: El Poblado
  • Neighborhood rhythm: Laureles
  • First decision: Busy evenings or a quieter base
  • Compare carefully: The street and room, not only the area

Choose the evening before the hotel

For a first Medellín trip, El Poblado and Laureles are useful starting points. Colombia’s tourism board describes El Poblado’s restaurants and nightlife and Laureles’ neighborhood atmosphere. Neither label makes every address interchangeable.

Start with the Medellín destination hub and our first-timer’s guide. Then ask a practical question: when you return after sightseeing, do you want another busy evening nearby, or a more residential setting in which to settle?

El Poblado: let dining shape the stay

Put El Poblado first if restaurants and nightlife are central to the trip. Provenza and the Parque Lleras area feature in the hub’s evening suggestions, but the right choice is still the exact street and property.

Look at the route between the room and the places you expect to use. Ask whether the room faces a busy street, whether there are stairs or steep approaches, and how you would return after dinner. If sleep is the priority, do not choose solely because a listing promises proximity to nightlife. Ask for a room-specific answer about noise.

Laureles: make room for ordinary mornings

Laureles is worth comparing if you want a more local, residential atmosphere and a café-led start to the day. The point is to choose a neighborhood you want to spend time in, rather than treating the hotel as somewhere to leave as quickly as possible.

Use the city’s official Vive Laureles and Vive el Poblado guides to compare cultural and dining ideas. Mark a few on a map before booking. Check the particular street, nearby evening activity and your likely transport needs; “Laureles” alone is not a guarantee of quiet.

Keep sightseeing separate from the base decision

You do not need to sleep beside every experience. Give Comuna 13’s culture and street art a deliberate place in the itinerary, whichever neighborhood you choose. Compare the walk’s focus, guide, meeting point and physical demands before reserving.

A useful short-stay structure is one neighborhood introduction, one main cultural outing and a flexible block for whatever you want more of. If you add Guatapé, leave it its own day rather than squeezing it between city appointments. The first-timer’s guide and destination hub provide the wider trip ideas.

Questions to send before booking

  • Room location: which floor and which side of the building will you receive?
  • Arrival: how does check-in work if your flight is delayed?
  • Transport: where is the actual pickup point for transfers and tours?
  • Access: are stairs, slopes or other access limitations relevant to the room?
  • Terms: what is included, and what happens if your plans change?

For a short visit, our suggestion is to keep one base and explore the other area as an outing. Switching hotels makes more sense when the change itself improves the trip, not simply to sample both names.

Continue through Colombia

Pair Medellín with the Bogotá hub for another city chapter or the Cartagena hub for the Caribbean coast. Read La Candelaria’s historic-heart guide before shaping a Bogotá stop, or our Cartagena neighborhood comparison if your next decision is another hotel base.

title: Pepa Pombo in Bogotá: The Sculptural Knitwear Shaping Colombian Style
dek: Inside the family-run house turning Colombian knitwear into color, architecture and the most effortless kind of statement dressing.
body:
Fashion Strolls · Bogotá, Colombia

Pepa Pombo in Bogotá

Bogotá style has always understood the drama of texture. Against the capital’s cool Andean light, Pepa Pombo’s knits feel especially alive: graphic, tactile and precise, yet designed with enough ease to move from a gallery afternoon to a candlelit dinner in Zona T.

Founded in 1978 by Pepa Pombo, the Colombian ready-to-wear house has spent decades reinventing knitwear. Today, daughter Mónica Holguín leads the design language as creative director, carrying a family story forward through dimensional surfaces, sculptural silhouettes and exuberant color.

A Colombian language of knit

The magic is in the construction. Instead of treating knit as a quiet basic, Pepa Pombo uses it as architecture. In-house production and handwoven techniques create three-dimensional textures that hold shape without losing softness. The result is clothing that reads beautifully from across a room and rewards a closer look.

For travelers, that balance is irresistible. Many pieces are multifunctional and forgiving to pack, while bold pattern does the styling work for you. It is a wardrobe proposition built around fewer, more memorable pieces.

The statement layerLook for an Astor or Nolita jacket: polished over a silk slip, relaxed with dark denim.

The graphic separateA Portico skirt or Celina blouse brings movement and visual rhythm without feeling costume-like.

The travel formulaAnchor one vivid knit with espresso, ivory or ink-black accessories and let texture lead.

Where to shop in Bogotá

The brand’s Bogotá boutiques include Carrera 14 #83-46 and Calle 79B #7-97, placing the experience close to the city’s fashionable northern neighborhoods. Hours can change, so confirm directly before visiting. If your route continues beyond Colombia, the house also lists boutiques and stockists in Cali, Mexico City, San Miguel de Allende and international destinations.

Jet Set LatAM styling note: Pack the knit flat rather than hanging it, add a slim leather loafer for daytime, then switch to a sculptural earring and heel after dark. For more Colombian fashion, continue with our guide to Johanna Ortiz in Cali.

Why it belongs in the modern travel wardrobe

Pepa Pombo’s strongest pieces are joyful but intentional. The house has discussed recycled polyester, certified renewable sources for rayon and viscose, and the value of timeless silhouettes—an approach that suits travelers who want personality without disposable trend-chasing.

In Bogotá, wear a textured jacket over a fine-gauge turtleneck for the city’s changeable temperatures. In Cartagena, reinterpret the same piece over a fluid dress. The pleasure is in discovering how one expressive garment can change across climates and occasions.

Style every journey

Build the look in Luxe Jetter

Use Luxe Jetter as the fashion and packing layer for your next Latin American escape—from statement knits to the shoes and finishing pieces that make them travel beautifully.

Open Luxe Jetter

If the app does not appear, explore Luxe Jetter here.

The final word

Pepa Pombo makes a compelling case for clothing as a souvenir of place—not a logo, but a point of view. These are knits with Bogotá intelligence and Colombian optimism: distinctive enough to remember, versatile enough to keep traveling.

Sources: Pepa Pombo official brand universe, boutique directory, current collection and sustainability editorial. Details verified September 2026; confirm store hours before travel.

title: Three Days in Antigua Guatemala: A Flexible First-Visit Itinerary
dek: Give the city a full day, leave space for coffee country, and resist turning every volcano into a checklist.
body:
How to use this itinerary

This is a suggested three-day shape for a first Antigua visit, not a timed tour or a promise that every activity fits every arrival. It draws on our Antigua first-timer’s guide: the historic center, coffee farms and the surrounding volcano country.

Stay near Parque Central if you want a walkable base. Keep your arrival and departure arrangements outside the busiest sightseeing plans: the journey from Guatemala City’s airport depends on traffic, and a prearranged transfer is worth organizing before you land.

Day one: settle into the historic center

Begin with Parque Central and the surrounding colonial arcades, then make the Santa Catalina Arch your next anchor. On a clear morning, Volcán de Agua forms the backdrop to the arch. Leave room to notice the streets and courtyards between your stops.

Choose ruined churches or convents as the second focus rather than trying to see every building in a single circuit. Antigua’s history is part of the experience of walking through it. Comfortable shoes help with the uneven cobblestones, and layers suit the cooler highland mornings and evenings.

If you arrive late, shorten this day to a stroll near your accommodation and carry the rest into tomorrow. The itinerary works better with a little flexibility than with a rushed first afternoon.

Day two: coffee country, then an open afternoon

Use the second day for a coffee-farm visit around Antigua, where tours explain the journey from cherry to cup. Before booking, ask which parts of the farm or production process are included, how you reach the meeting point and how long to allow. Do not assume every visit offers the same experience.

For background, Guatemala’s cultural information system describes the coffee museum at La Azotea. Use the official listing as a starting point for checking a current visit, not as a guarantee of a particular tour schedule.

Leave the afternoon for a courtyard pause and the historic-center stops you missed. That breathing room is useful if weather or transport changes the morning plan.

Day three: choose one direction

Make the final day a choice rather than a stack of excursions. You might stay in town and explore more slowly, or arrange a guided outing into the surrounding landscape. Pacaya appears in our first-timer’s guide as a volcano option; ask a reputable guide about the current route, conditions and demands before deciding it fits your party.

For another perspective on the region, read our mountain biking in Guatemala story. Choose an activity around your experience and available time, rather than adding it simply because it appears on a list.

Lake Atitlán is a popular onward stop a few hours away; our recommendation is to give it its own stay rather than making it a compulsory dash from Antigua.

Pack a rain jacket for May–October, confirm excursion details close to the date, and keep some unbooked time. Three days can be a satisfying introduction without trying to cover all of Guatemala.

title: Where to Stay in San Juan: Old San Juan, Condado or Ocean Park?
dek: History at your doorstep or a beach-led stay? Start with that choice, then build the rest of San Juan around it.
body:
Choose your everyday setting

Where to stay in San Juan depends on what you want to do without turning it into a whole excursion. Choose Old San Juan if the historic streets are the heart of your visit. Compare Condado and Ocean Park if beach time belongs in most of your days.

For a first trip, our suggestion is to choose a primary mood and visit the other side of the city deliberately. You can enjoy both without assuming every neighborhood needs an overnight stay. Start with the San Juan first-timer’s guide for the full set of places and flavors.

Old San Juan: put history first

Old San Juan brings pastel colonial streets, blue cobblestones and the Atlantic-facing forts of El Morro and San Cristóbal into your daily setting. It is the clearest choice if wandering the old city matters more to you than beginning each morning by the beach.

Build your first full day around the historic center and leave room for a long pause. Before booking, check the exact address and ask about anything your party needs for comfortable access, including stairs and luggage arrival. A beautiful historic building and the right room for your trip are separate decisions.

Condado: beach time with city conveniences

Condado is the beachfront hotel area, with restaurants and a lagoon used for paddleboarding. It suits a trip that alternates time outdoors with meals and city exploring. Discover Puerto Rico’s Condado guide describes the neighborhood’s beach, lagoon and shopping options.

When comparing stays, distinguish an oceanfront address from a short walk to the shore. Ask what beach access and facilities the property actually provides. Ocean conditions vary; follow local flags and lifeguard guidance rather than choosing a swimming spot from hotel photographs.

Ocean Park—and room for Santurce

Ocean Park is another beach base to compare alongside Condado. Use the actual accommodation address to work out how your beach time, meals and outings will fit together, rather than choosing purely by the neighborhood label.

Santurce adds murals, galleries and La Placita’s lively evenings to the trip. Even if you sleep by the beach or in the old city, give this creative side of San Juan a place in your plans. Choose a few priorities and arrange the return journey before the evening gets going.

One stay or a split stay?

Some visitors divide their time between the old city and the beach. Our recommendation for a short visit is to start with one base: changing rooms costs time, even when both areas appeal. A split stay makes more sense if you have enough days to settle into each setting and you actively want two different experiences.

Keep day trips selective, too. El Yunque and the bioluminescent lagoon at Fajardo are both in the first-timer’s guide, but they need space around the rest of your plans. Check pickup locations, return arrangements and current access before reserving.

Compare accommodation after deciding whether history or beach time comes first.

title: Antigua Guatemala: A First-Timer’s Guide
dek: Cobbled lanes, courtyard stays and coffee country, with volcanoes on the horizon.
body:
Framed by three volcanoes, Antigua Guatemala is one of the best-preserved colonial towns in the Americas and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its cobbled grid of pastel houses, ruined churches and courtyards makes it the natural first stop in Guatemala — and a base for volcano hikes, coffee farms and Lake Atitlán.

First Trip at a Glance

  • Walkable base: Near Parque Central
  • First sights: Santa Catalina Arch and ruined churches
  • Beyond town: Coffee farms and guided volcano hikes
  • Pack well: Cobblestone shoes and highland layers

What to see

  • The Santa Catalina Arch — the yellow arch on Calle del Arco, with Volcán de Agua behind it on a clear morning.
  • The ruined churches and convents — earthquakes left many of Antigua’s colonial buildings as atmospheric ruins you can walk through.
  • Parque Central — the leafy main square, surrounded by the cathedral and colonial arcades.

Volcanoes and coffee

For a café stop in town, compare Fernando’s Kaffee and Café Condesa in our Antigua breakfast and coffee guide, with direct venue links and a flexible two-morning plan.

Pacaya is the easiest volcano hike from town. For the adventurous, an overnight hike up Acatenango offers views of neighboring Fuego, one of Central America’s most active volcanoes. The hills around Antigua are coffee country, and farm tours explain the journey from cherry to cup. Always hike with a reputable guide. See also our story on mountain biking in Guatemala.

Where to stay

Boutique hotels in restored colonial houses are Antigua’s signature: courtyards, fountains and bougainvillea. Stay within a few blocks of Parque Central so everything is walkable.

Find a stay that fits your base and pace.

title: San Juan, Puerto Rico: A First-Timer’s Guide
dek: A first taste of Puerto Rico: old-city streets, beach time and a table full of local flavor.
body:
San Juan combines a five-century-old walled city with city beaches, a serious food scene and some of the best day trips in the Caribbean. For US citizens it is also one of the easiest escapes in the region — no passport required, and the currency is the US dollar.

First Trip at a Glance

  • History base: Old San Juan
  • Beach base: Condado or Ocean Park
  • On the table: Mofongo, lechón and alcapurrias
  • Drier season: December–April

The neighborhoods

  • Old San Juan — pastel colonial streets, blue cobblestones, and the massive forts of El Morro and San Cristóbal overlooking the Atlantic.
  • Condado — the beachfront hotel strip, with restaurants and a lagoon for paddleboarding.
  • Santurce — the creative quarter, known for street murals, galleries and La Placita’s lively evenings.

Where to stay

Stay in Old San Juan for history and walkability, or Condado and neighboring Ocean Park for beach time. Many visitors split a trip between the two.

Find a stay that fits your base and pace.

Compare San Juan hotels ↗

Opens Booking.com in a new tab. Enter your destination and dates to search; availability varies.

What to eat

Planning meals around the historic district? Our Old San Juan coffee and lunch guide compares a focused shortlist, with links to current tourism and venue information.

Mofongo (mashed, fried plantain), lechón, alcapurrias from a roadside kiosk, and a piña colada in the city that claims to have invented it. The kiosks of Piñones, just east of the city, are a local favorite for fritters by the sea.

Day trips

El Yunque, the only tropical rainforest in the US National Forest System, is about an hour away, with waterfalls and trails. After dark, kayak tours visit the bioluminescent lagoon at Fajardo, where the water glows when disturbed.

Make room for a local experience. Check the itinerary and current availability before booking.

When to go

December to April is the driest, busiest season. The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to November, so travel insurance is worth considering then.

title: Santiago + Casablanca Valley: A Wine Country Weekend
dek: Chile is one of the world’s great wine countries, and Santiago is arguably the easiest base from which to experience it — several distinct valleys sit within an hour or two of the city, each with its own personality.
body:
Casablanca Valley — Closest & Coolest

About 45 minutes from Santiago toward the coast, Casablanca’s cooler climate makes it Chile’s go-to region for crisp Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay — a contrast to the bolder reds most people associate with Chilean wine. It’s an easy half-day or full-day trip, with several wineries open for tastings and tours.

Maipo Valley — Closer, Bolder

Maipo sits practically in Santiago’s backyard and is Chile’s most historic wine region, known for structured Cabernet Sauvignon. Concha y Toro, one of the world’s largest and most recognizable wine producers, is based here and offers public tours and tastings of its estate.

Colchagua Valley — Worth the Extra Distance

Roughly two hours south, Colchagua is worth it for travelers with an extra day — bigger, more polished estates and a wine-focused town (Santa Cruz) built around the industry.

Planning the Day

Most visitors book a half- or full-day tour rather than self-driving between wineries, since tastings and driving don’t mix. Book ahead in peak season (harvest runs March–April) and confirm tasting fees, which vary by estate.

title: First Timer’s Guide to Santiago
dek: Santiago doesn’t get the immediate name recognition of Buenos Aires or Rio, and that’s part of its appeal — a modern, efficient Andean capital that’s equal parts gateway city and destination in its own right, with some of South Am
body:
Santiago doesn’t get the immediate name recognition of Buenos Aires or Rio, and that’s part of its appeal — a modern, efficient Andean capital that’s equal parts gateway city and destination in its own right, with some of South America’s best wine country less than an hour away.

Getting Around

Santiago’s Metro is one of the best in Latin America — fast, clean, and easy to navigate. For views, take the funicular or cable car up Cerro San Cristóbal, the hill anchoring Bellavista.

Neighborhoods to Know

  • Lastarria — bohemian, walkable, full of cafés, galleries and bookshops
  • Providencia — leafy, residential, business-district practical
  • Bellavista — nightlife and color, home to Pablo Neruda’s La Chascona
  • Barrio Italia — design shops, antiques, and a slower pace

What to Eat

Try a completo (Chile’s elaborate hot dog, loaded with avocado, tomato and mayo) at least once, then head to the Mercado Central for fresh seafood — Chile’s Pacific coastline means ceviche and congrio here are the real thing.

Don’t Miss

  • Cerro San Cristóbal — the city’s best skyline and Andes views
  • Palacio de La Moneda — the presidential palace, with rotating art exhibitions in its cultural center
  • Casablanca Valley wine country — see our full itinerary below

When to Go

September–November and March–May are the sweet spots — mild weather without summer’s heat or winter’s smog. Grape harvest in the wine valleys runs March–April, if timing a wine trip is a priority.

title: La Candelaria: Bogotá’s Historic Heart
dek: La Candelaria is where Bogotá began — a grid of colonial streets, colorful balconied houses, and plazas that have anchored the city since the 1500s. It’s the most walkable introduction to the capital, and the neighborhood where it
body:
La Candelaria is where Bogotá began — a grid of colonial streets, colorful balconied houses, and plazas that have anchored the city since the 1500s. It’s the most walkable introduction to the capital, and the neighborhood where its museums, street art, and student energy all overlap.

Start at Plaza Bolívar

Bogotá’s central square is ringed by the Capitolio Nacional, the Palace of Justice, and the city’s cathedral — a good orientation point before wandering the surrounding streets.

Museums Within Walking Distance

La Candelaria holds an unusual concentration of world-class museums: the Museo del Oro, the Museo Botero, and the Museo Nacional are all a short walk from each other, making the neighborhood an easy full day on foot.

Chorro de Quevedo

Considered the founding site of Bogotá, this small plaza is now a hub of student cafés, street performers, and some of the neighborhood’s densest street art — worth slowing down for rather than rushing through.

A Practical Note

La Candelaria is best visited by day. It empties out and becomes noticeably less lively after dark — plan dinner elsewhere, in Chapinero or the Zona G.

title: First Timer’s Guide to Bogotá
dek: Bogotá sits at 8,660 feet in the Andes, which means your first afternoon should be slow — the altitude is real. Once you’ve adjusted, the reward is a capital that’s gritty and elegant in equal measure: colonial streets, world-clas
body:
Bogotá sits at 8,660 feet in the Andes, which means your first afternoon should be slow — the altitude is real. Once you’ve adjusted, the reward is a capital that’s gritty and elegant in equal measure: colonial streets, world-class museums, and a food and coffee scene with real depth.

Getting Around

The TransMilenio bus rapid transit system covers most of the city, but Uber and taxis are the easier option for visitors, especially at night. Traffic is heavy — budget more time than you think for cross-town trips.

Neighborhoods to Know

  • La Candelaria — the colonial historic center, museums, street art (full guide below)
  • Chapinero — creative, LGBTQ-friendly, strong nightlife and independent restaurants
  • Usaquén — upscale and colonial-village-like, with a beloved Sunday flea market
  • Zona T / Zona G — Bogotá’s dining and shopping core

What to Eat

Ajiaco — a hearty chicken and potato soup native to Bogotá — is the dish to order on a cold, rainy afternoon (of which there are many). Pair it with hot chocolate and cheese, chocolate santafereño, a genuinely strange and genuinely good local ritual. For produce, spices, and a real sense of the city’s food culture, spend an hour at Paloquemao market.

Don’t Miss

  • Museo del Oro (Gold Museum) — one of the best museums in South America
  • Monserrate — cable car or funicular up to a mountaintop church with sweeping city views
  • Museo Botero — Fernando Botero’s own collection, free to enter

When to Go

Bogotá’s climate is mild and fairly consistent year-round, so it rarely dictates timing. December is a genuine highlight, when the city’s Christmas light displays (los Alumbrados) turn parks and rivers into elaborate installations.

title: Comuna 13 & Medellín’s Culture of Transformation
dek: No neighborhood tells Medellín’s story like Comuna 13. Once considered one of the most dangerous places in the world, it’s now an open-air museum of street art, outdoor escalators, and hip-hop culture — built, quite literally, by
body:
No neighborhood tells Medellín’s story like Comuna 13. Once considered one of the most dangerous places in the world, it’s now an open-air museum of street art, outdoor escalators, and hip-hop culture — built, quite literally, by the community that lived through its hardest years.

Why the Escalators Matter

Installed in 2011, the outdoor escalators were a public infrastructure project meant to connect a hillside neighborhood cut off by geography and violence. They became a symbol of the city’s transformation — and today they’re lined with murals, graffiti, and vendors, climbing past homes that once sat at the center of the conflict.

What to Expect

Local guides — many of whom grew up in the neighborhood — lead walking tours that combine the history with the art, plus impromptu breakdance and hip-hop performances along the route. Go with a guide rather than alone; the context they add is most of the point. Wear comfortable shoes for the stairs and hills.

Respectful Visiting

This is a residential neighborhood with a difficult history, not a theme park. Ask before photographing people directly, tip your guide, and buy something from the vendors and artists along the way — tourism here is directly tied to the community’s economic recovery.

Pair It With

Comuna 13 is a half-day outing. Combine it with the Jardín Botánico or a Metrocable ride up to Parque Arví to round out the day.

title: First Timer’s Guide to Medellín
dek: Medellín has spent the last two decades rewriting its story — from a city defined by conflict to Latin America’s most talked-about urban comeback. What draws people back is the climate first (a permanent, spring-like 70°F thanks t
body:
Medellín has spent the last two decades rewriting its story — from a city defined by conflict to Latin America’s most talked-about urban comeback. What draws people back is the climate first (a permanent, spring-like 70°F thanks to the Aburrá Valley’s elevation), then the food, the art, and a pace of life that feels genuinely livable. Here’s what to know before you land.

Getting Around

The Metro is Medellín’s pride and joy — clean, cheap, and the backbone of the city, extending into the hills via the Metrocable gondola lines that double as genuine tourist attractions. For everything else, Uber and taxis are inexpensive and reliable.

Where to Base Yourself

El Poblado is the upscale, walkable base most first-timers choose — leafy streets, boutique hotels, the city’s best restaurants, and a buzzy nightlife scene around Parque Lleras. Laureles is the local alternative: quieter, more residential, better value, and arguably more authentic, with its own strong café and restaurant scene around Segundo Parque.

What to Eat

Start with bandeja paisa — the iconic regional plate of beans, rice, avocado, chorizo, and more. Arepas here are their own regional style, thicker and often topped rather than filled. For a modern take on Colombian ingredients, Medellín’s tasting-menu scene has grown into one of South America’s most interesting.

Don’t Miss

  • Comuna 13 — outdoor escalators and street art in a neighborhood that transformed itself (full guide below)
  • Parque Arví — a cable car ride up into cloud forest and hiking trails
  • Jardín Botánico — free, lush, and an easy afternoon
  • Pueblito Paisa — a hilltop replica village with the best skyline view in the city

When to Go

Medellín’s climate barely changes year-round, so timing comes down to events — the Feria de las Flores (Flower Festival) each August fills the city with parades and, fittingly, flowers.

title: Pan de Muerto in Mexico City: A Beautiful Ritual of Memory and Sweetness
dek: Orange blossom, butter and sugar turn a seasonal loaf into one of Mexico City’s most meaningful autumn rituals.
body:
Sweet Strolls · Mexico City

Pan de Muerto, Memory Made Delicious

By late September, Mexico City begins to glow in marigold tones. Bakeries perfume the sidewalks with orange zest and anise, café tables fill with sugar-dusted rounds, and the first pan de muerto of the season becomes a small ceremony of anticipation. This is not simply a pastry trend. It is a bread made for remembrance, placed on ofrendas and shared with the living as Día de Muertos approaches on November 1 and 2.

In the capital, the classic version is softly domed and crossed with slender pieces of dough often read as bones, finished with butter and a generous coat of sugar. Its crumb is tender and fragrant rather than overly sweet. The pleasure is in the contrast: a delicate crust, a pillowy center and the brightness of orange blossom against warm spice.

A tradition with many histories

Mexico’s Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia offers a useful correction to the simplest origin stories. The modern Día de Muertos celebration carries multiple historical layers, including medieval European Catholic observances that evolved in Mexico alongside distinct Indigenous traditions. Bread, sweets, flowers, fruit and prepared dishes became part of the offerings that families assemble to welcome and honor the dead.

Regional breads make the tradition richer still. An INAH study documents forms ranging from roscas de la vida and butter “bones” to breads shaped as people, animals and plants. In San Pablito, Puebla, anthropomorphic breads decorated with vegetable color represent the souls of the departed and may be served with cacao atole. Mexico City’s sugared round is only one beautiful expression in a much larger edible language.

Jet Set LatAM note: Approach pan de muerto as a seasonal ritual, not a checklist item. Order one loaf to share, ask which version the bakery makes, and notice how scent, shape and texture carry meaning.

What to order in Mexico City

The classic

Choose a traditional sugar-coated loaf scented with orange blossom. Tear it by hand and pair it with café de olla or hot chocolate.

The filled

Contemporary bakeries add nata, chocolate, dulce de leche or seasonal creams. Share one after tasting the classic first.

The regional

Seek bakeries and markets presenting breads from Puebla, Oaxaca or other regions; shapes and flavorings can change dramatically.

A slow, stylish bakery morning

Begin in Roma Norte or Condesa, where a bakery crawl can unfold on foot between leafy streets and design shops. Go early for the widest selection and a calmer counter. Order one pan for the table, then take another carefully boxed for later. Continue the day through the city with our Mexico City destination guide, or make the morning part of a design-and-boutique walk through Roma Norte.

Dress for a long city stroll: easy trousers, a light knit, polished flats and a structured tote with room for a bakery box. In late October and early November, mornings can feel fresh while afternoons warm, so a removable layer is more useful than a heavy coat.

How to taste respectfully

Día de Muertos is an active cultural and family observance. Photograph public installations and bakery displays freely where permitted, but ask before photographing private altars or intimate ceremonies. Buy from independent neighborhood bakeries when possible, and remember that the bread on an ofrenda is part of remembrance before it is content.

For travelers arriving outside the peak season, ask about other celebratory breads rather than expecting pan de muerto year-round. Seasonality is part of its meaning. During autumn, popular bakeries may sell out, so preorder large or specialty loaves and verify current hours directly.

Save the sweet moment

Find your next beautiful bite with Let Them Eat

Use Let Them Eat to remember the bakeries, cakes and destination sweets worth crossing a city for.

Discover Let Them Eat on the App Store

A loaf that keeps a place at the table

Pan de muerto is joyful without forgetting why it exists. Its scent can fill a fashionable café, a neighborhood bakery or a family home, yet the gesture remains the same: make something beautiful, place memory at the center, and share sweetness with the people who are here. In Mexico City, that first sugared bite is one of autumn’s most tender invitations.

Sources: INAH — El origen del Día de Muertos; INAH — Pan de muerto tradicional de San Pablito; Visit México — Día de Muertos.

title: Buenos Aires in December: Tango, Style & 3-Day Itinerary
dek: The Jet Set Journal: Summer, Style, and Late-Night Tango in Buenos Aires
body:
There is never a bad time to visit Buenos Aires, but December hits differently. settles over the grand avenues, café tables spill onto the sidewalks, and the city stays awake long after anyone sensible has gone to bed. December 11 marks Argentina’s National Tango Day, making this an especially fitting month to experience the dance in the city that shaped it.

Consider this your Jet Set field guide to Buenos Aires in December: what to wear, where to wander, how to approach your first milonga, and what to eat when you emerge at two in the morning.

Quick Links

  • What to Pack
  • 3-Day Buenos Aires Itinerary
  • Tango and Milongas
  • What to Eat
  • Plan With the Jet Set App Family

The Luxe Jetter Edit: What to Pack for a Tango Summer

December in Buenos Aires is hot, and the city’s style tends to make casual clothing look considerably more intentional than it has any right to.

Think breathable fabrics, uncomplicated silhouettes, good shoes, and pieces capable of moving from an afternoon café to a very late dinner.

For the Milonga

For followers, a lightweight A-line or midi dress gives you movement without requiring a full costume moment. Linen blends, rayon, silk blends, and other breathable fabrics work well in the summer heat.

For leaders, lightweight trousers or chinos with a breathable button-down or polished polo are considerably more practical than heavy suiting.

Bring a small dance bag with a hand fan, dance shoes, and an extra top. A packed dance hall and Buenos Aires summer are an ambitious combination.

Need help building the rest of the suitcase? Explore destination-inspired looks in Luxe Jetter on the App Store.

For Exploring the City

During the day, keep things simple: linen sundresses, cotton tees, tailored shorts, lightweight trousers, sunglasses, and serious sunscreen.

Buenos Aires rewards walking, but historic sidewalks are not always friendly to beautiful shoes. Save the heels for later and wear supportive leather sandals or clean sneakers while exploring.

Three Days of Rallii + Rhythm

Day One: The Soul of San Telmo

Afternoon: Begin in San Telmo. Wander its cobblestone streets, old architecture, interior courtyards, antique shops, and independent studios. Give yourself permission to have nowhere particularly urgent to be.

Evening: Make your first tango night about experiencing a real milonga rather than simply watching tango performed. If you are completely new to the culture, a local guide or introductory experience can help explain traditions such as the cabeceo, the subtle eye contact and nod historically used to invite someone to dance.

Day Two: Café Culture and Late Nights

Afternoon: Visit historic Café Tortoni for coffee and something sweet, then spend the afternoon walking through central Buenos Aires.

Night: This is the night to go deeper. Take a class, find a neighborhood milonga, and experience the version of tango that exists beyond the big theatrical productions.

Do not plan an aggressive 8 a.m. itinerary for the following morning. Buenos Aires has other ideas for you.

Day Three: Palermo Design and Grand Tango

Daytime: Head to Palermo Soho for independent fashion, leather goods, design stores, cafés, and a completely different side of the city from historic San Telmo.

If tango has already gotten under your skin, this is also the day to look for locally made dance shoes.

Evening: Finish with spectacle. After experiencing tango socially, see its theatrical side with a stage production featuring professional dancers, musicians, and a live orchestra.

Keep exploring beyond the obvious stops. Discover Rallii on the App Store.

A Note About Tango Etiquette

A milonga is a social dance event, not simply a tango show. Traditional spaces can have their own rhythms and etiquette around invitations, seating, dance sets, and navigating the floor.

You do not need to arrive knowing everything. You do need to arrive curious.

Take a beginner lesson, observe the room, follow the venue’s norms, and remember that you are stepping into a living local tradition rather than an attraction created solely for visitors.

Let Them Eat: Buenos Aires After Dark

You’ve danced until midnight. Naturally, dinner is just getting interesting.

Buenos Aires operates on a clock that begins to make perfect sense after about forty-eight hours in the city.

Start with vermouth and something salty. Order the steak if you eat meat, or explore the city’s Italian-influenced pasta, pizza, provoleta, and vegetable dishes. Have the flan with dulce de leche even though everyone at the table claimed they were full.

And keep an alfajor nearby for tomorrow.

Empanadas are the ideal bridge between sightseeing, dancing, and the realization that your next proper meal may happen considerably later than expected.

A good trip does not begin at the airport. Discover the destination, build the wardrobe, find the experiences, and decide what you are eating long before wheels up.

title: Carla Fernández in Mexico City: The Square-Root Language of Modern Mexican Fashion
dek: The Mexico City city guide — where to stay, eat and wander  ·  The perfect 3-day Mexico City itinerary  ·  Next stop: Oaxaca or Guadalajara
body:
Mexico City dresses in layers of time. In Roma Norte, a morning walk can move from Porfirian façades to contemporary galleries, a tiled courtyard and a fashion studio where geometry carries centuries of knowledge. At Carla Fernández, the most radical silhouette often begins with the oldest idea: a square of cloth, left legible. The Mexico City fashion house treats Indigenous and mestizo textile heritage as a living design language. Its clothes are architectural but never cold, exuberant without becoming costume, and grounded in collaborations with makers across Mexico.

A Fashion Stroll Through Roma Norte

Begin near Álvaro Obregón, where tree-lined medians, bookshops and cafés establish Roma Norte’s unhurried rhythm. The brand’s official site lists an address at Álvaro Obregón 200, making the atelier-boutique a natural anchor for a design-led afternoon. Continue the neighborhood exploration with our guide to the best designer boutiques in Mexico City, which places Carla Fernández among Roma’s independent labels and concept stores. Give the clothes time. Their intelligence appears in the placement of a fold, the width of a rectangular panel and the way a woven story remains uninterrupted. Ask who made the textile, which community and technique it comes from, and how the garment was developed collaboratively.

The Fashion House and Its Collaborative Practice

Carla Fernández is a Mexico City-based fashion and textile house dedicated to preserving and revitalizing the textile legacy of Mexico’s Indigenous and mestizo communities. According to the brand, its designs are co-created with more than 175 weavers, embroiderers, woodcarvers, leatherworkers, cutwork artisans and dyers across twelve Mexican states. The atelier describes embroidery and hand weaving as integral to design and production, not decoration applied at the end. Its work has been presented in solo exhibitions at institutions including Museo Jumex, the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum and the Fashion Institute of Technology. The company has also been a certified B Corporation since 2018, using the framework to evaluate governance, workers, community and environmental impact.

Understanding La Raíz Cuadrada

The house calls its pattern-making method la raíz cuadrada—the square root. Where Western tailoring often cuts curves to follow the body, many Indigenous Mexican garments join square and rectangular textile panels through folds, pleats and seams. Fernández compares this construction to textile origami. The method is beautiful because it respects the fabric as an archive. A woven panel can be read like an open book: cutting through it risks dividing the maker’s visual narrative. By working from the textile’s geometry, the garment preserves more of that story while producing a striking contemporary volume.

Pieces and Techniques to Notice

Start with the huipil, poncho or cape, silhouettes that make the square-root system immediately visible. Notice how generous planes of cloth create movement without conventional darting. A rebozo tunic woven on a treadle loom can fall with soft authority; a cutwork charro poncho turns negative space into ornament; an embroidered blouse carries intimate detail within a disciplined shape. Accessories reveal another side of the house. Tecuán bags reference traditional masks through hand-worked leather, while tin milagro earrings translate devotional forms into playful, lightweight punctuation. Because hand processes create natural variations, color and texture may differ slightly from the screen—evidence of making, not imperfection.

Visiting and Shopping Thoughtfully

Confirm current opening hours or arrange a visit directly before going. For pieces made to order, the official site asks customers to allow three to four weeks of production in addition to shipping. If a garment is intended for a specific journey, inquire early and confirm international delivery, duties and return terms. Ask about fiber, region, technique and maker collaboration before choosing. A wardrobe built slowly benefits from care instructions as much as styling advice: woven and embroidered pieces may need gentle hand washing, flat storage or specialist cleaning. Fold structured textiles along their natural construction lines and protect embellishment inside a breathable cloth bag.

The Jet Set LatAM Styling Edit

For Mexico City, pair a graphic huipil with long black trousers, a narrow leather sandal and sculptural silver earrings. Let a voluminous cape sharpen a fitted column dress after dark. A rebozo tunic feels modern over cream denim with an oxblood bag, while a Tecuán accessory brings wit to an otherwise restrained travel uniform. The key is proportion. Balance one generous geometric shape with a clean line elsewhere, repeat a single color from the textile and resist over-accessorizing. The clothes already contain architecture, history and motion; styling should give those elements room to breathe.

CONTINUE THE FASHION STROLL

Style Mexico City with Luxe Jetter

Build a city wardrobe around architectural layers, artisan textiles and polished pieces made for long, beautiful walks.

Open Luxe Jetter in Its Own Page ✦

A Future Built from Living Knowledge

Carla Fernández demonstrates that preservation and experimentation do not sit on opposite sides of fashion. The square can become a cape, a tunic, a statement or a quiet everyday layer without surrendering the textile’s memory. In Roma Norte, the house offers travelers something rarer than a souvenir: a way to see Mexican design as an evolving conversation between geometry, community and the hand. Sources: Carla Fernández — About Us; Carla Fernández — Nosotrxs; Carla Fernández — Styles and Square Root; Carla Fernández — Textile and Materials Workshop.

title: Silvia Furmanovich in São Paulo: Brazilian Marquetry Becomes Fine Jewelry
dek: The São Paulo city guide — where to stay, eat and wander  ·  The perfect 3-day São Paulo itinerary  ·  Next stop: Rio de Janeiro
body:
São Paulo reveals its most captivating luxury in the tension between polish and experiment. Behind an appointment-only atelier door, precious stones meet native Brazilian woods, miniature mosaics and the patient intelligence of the hand. This is the world of Silvia Furmanovich: exuberant, exacting and impossible to mistake for anyone else’s. For travelers who read a city through what it makes, her jewelry offers a particularly vivid portrait of Brazil. Color is fearless, scale is confident and traditional craft is never treated as nostalgia. Instead, it becomes the beginning of something modern.

A Jewelry-Led Fashion Stroll Through São Paulo

Begin in São Paulo with the city’s appetite for design: modernist architecture, tropical gardens, galleries and boutiques that reward a slower eye. Our guide to the best designer boutiques in São Paulo’s Jardins district makes a natural companion to this story, placing Brazilian fashion within one of the city’s most elegant neighborhoods. Furmanovich’s official website lists her Brazil atelier as available to visit by request. An appointment is the right rhythm for work this intricate. It allows time to look beyond sparkle and notice the construction: a precise hinge, the meeting of wood and gold, or a motif assembled from tiny veneers.

The Designer and Her São Paulo Story

Born in São Paulo into a family of Italian goldsmiths, Silvia Furmanovich learned the importance of craftsmanship from her father. She established her appointment-only jewelry business in 1998 and opened her first standalone São Paulo boutique in 2009. More than twenty-five years after launching the brand, the family company remains based in the city while maintaining an international presence. Her visual language is shaped by travel, natural materials and sustained collaboration with artists and artisans. Wood marquetry, ebony, oxidized copper, vintage lacquer, shells, woven bamboo and miniature painting appear beside yellow and rose gold, diamonds and Brazil’s vivid colored gemstones. The contrast is central to the magic: humble and precious, earthy and luminous, ancient technique and contemporary form.

Marquetry: A Brazilian Signature

The Marquetry collection began after Furmanovich traveled to Acre, Brazil’s westernmost state, and encountered craftspeople working with native woods. The technique assembles hand-cut wood veneers into intricate pictures and patterns. In Furmanovich’s jewelry, flora, fauna and trompe-l’œil gemstones emerge from reclaimed fragments of richly colored wood. The official collection story names woods including red Muirapiranga, yellow Tatajuba, green Louro Abacate, purple Roxinho and blue Azul Carvalho. Their natural tones are enhanced with water and minerals, then paired with amethyst, citrine, topaz, peridot, moonstone, beryl, prasiolite, fire opal, garnet and smoky quartz. Wood also keeps dramatic earrings surprisingly light—a practical luxury worth appreciating when packing for evenings out.

Pieces and Details to Notice

Look first for a pair of statement earrings. Furmanovich’s scale can be theatrical, but the craftsmanship makes the drama feel disciplined. Botanical and winged motifs bring movement near the face; geometric compositions show how naturally marquetry converses with Art Deco lines. Brooches are another expressive entry point. Pin one to the lapel of a white dinner jacket, the waist of a silk dress or the ribbon of a wide-brimmed hat. A cocktail ring offers concentrated color, while a marquetry clutch turns an evening accessory into a miniature cabinet of wonders. Across collections such as Kashmir, Amazonia Bamboo and Around the World, ask how a particular technique entered the studio’s vocabulary. Furmanovich’s monograph describes a practice of traveling to learn time-honored crafts—from miniature painting in India to bamboo work in Japan and marquetry in Brazil—and building close relationships with skilled makers.

Planning an Atelier Visit or Purchase

Request a Brazil atelier visit through the contact details on the official website before your trip. Availability, pricing and lead times should be confirmed directly, especially for one-of-a-kind work. If buying internationally, ask about insured shipping, duties, returns and documentation before committing. Fine jewelry deserves thoughtful travel habits. Keep pieces in separate soft pouches, carry them rather than checking them, and follow the atelier’s care guidance for mixed materials. Wood, lacquer, bamboo and miniature painting may require different handling from conventional gold-and-gemstone jewelry.

The Jet Set LatAM Styling Edit

The fashion-forward approach is restraint around one extraordinary object. For a Jardins lunch, pair sculptural marquetry earrings with an ivory column dress, a tobacco suede bag and flat leather sandals. At night, let a botanical brooch punctuate a sharply tailored black suit. For a gallery afternoon, wear a vivid cocktail ring with a crisp poplin shirt and fluid chocolate trousers. Avoid matching every color in the jewel. Choose one quiet echo—a lipstick shade, a sandal or a silk scarf—and let the craftsmanship hold the room. São Paulo style is most compelling when sophistication leaves space for surprise.

Jewelry as a Passport to Craft

Silvia Furmanovich transforms jewelry into a record of encounter. Her pieces carry São Paulo’s creative confidence, Acre’s woods, a goldsmith’s precision and the knowledge of makers across continents. To wear one is not simply to add ornament. It is to carry a small, radiant archive of material, place and human skill. title: Kika Vargas in Bogotá: Romantic Volume with a Modern Colombian Edge
dek: Translate Kika Vargas’s romantic volume into a destination-ready edit for galleries, dinners and cool Bogotá evenings.
body:
Bogotá dresses in layers: cool morning air, sudden sun, a gallery opening that becomes dinner. It is the perfect city for the expressive silhouettes of Kika Vargas, where clouds of taffeta, crisp cotton and artful proportion transform a practical wardrobe into something delightfully unexpected. The Colombian designer’s language is romantic but never passive. A sleeve may bloom beyond the shoulder, a skirt may gather into sculptural volume, or a restrained palette may sharpen the drama of a single extraordinary shape. These are clothes that understand the pleasure of an entrance—and the intelligence of editing everything around it.

A Bogotá Fashion Stroll

Begin in the northern neighborhoods where Bogotá’s fashion, restaurants and galleries share the same polished energy. The city’s altitude and mercurial weather reward a wardrobe that can shift: a statement blouse beneath a clean coat, a generous dress grounded by a practical shoe, a dramatic skirt softened with knitwear. Continue the Colombian fashion conversation with our Silvia Tcherassi guide to Cartagena. The contrast is revealing. Caribbean ease becomes metropolitan structure, yet both designers understand color, movement and the confidence of a woman who does not need to disappear into her clothes.

The Kika Vargas Point of View

Kika Vargas has become one of the Colombian names most closely associated with modern statement dressing. Her collections build emotion through silhouette rather than excess decoration: sleeves curve away from the body, skirts hold their own architecture, and familiar shirting is recut with a sense of theater. The label’s international presence is part of the story. Its official stockist list includes leading online retailers such as Net-a-Porter, Saks Fifth Avenue, Shopbop, SSENSE, Revolve and Rent the Runway, along with boutiques in the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Hong Kong, Mexico and St. Barth. That reach makes the clothes accessible far beyond Bogotá while keeping their Colombian identity central.

Pieces to Notice

The Voluminous Dress

The dress is the most immediate expression of the house. Look for silhouettes that balance a fitted point—at the neck, waist or cuff—with expansive fabric elsewhere. Current names such as the Tsige, Birgit, Billie and Alanna dresses suggest the breadth of the collection, from streamlined evening ease to fuller, more architectural forms.

The Statement Top

A Kika Vargas blouse or shirt may be the smartest travel purchase. The Hope, Ioanna, Agnes, Ambika and Harpa styles show how one upper layer can change trousers already in your suitcase. In cotton, crepe, nylon or taffeta, these pieces deliver impact without requiring an entirely new look.

The Sculptural Separate

Skirts and trousers make the volume easier to remix. A gathered midi skirt with a fine-gauge sweater feels quietly artistic; a wide trouser beside a precise top creates a confident proportion that works from a museum afternoon to a long dinner.

How to Shop the Collection

The official online store currently presents Fall/Winter 2026 alongside new arrivals, dresses, tops and bottoms. Product pages list prices in U.S. dollars, while the stockist directory offers alternatives for travelers who prefer to try pieces in person. Because statement silhouettes depend on proportion, check each garment’s measurements rather than relying only on your usual size. When shopping remotely, study the fabrication and movement in every image. Taffeta holds volume differently from cotton; crepe falls closer to the body. Confirm shipping, returns and any destination duties before ordering, and contact the retailer directly for the most current availability.

The Jet Set LatAM Styling Edit

For Bogotá, pair a sculptural blouse with charcoal trousers, a long wool coat and a slim leather boot. Let a full dress meet a flat or low-heeled shoe so the styling feels contemporary rather than ceremonial. A single oversized earring or compact top-handle bag is enough; the silhouette already provides the jewelry. For warm-weather travel, choose a crisp cotton dress and keep the accessories lean: barely-there sandals, a woven clutch and one bold cuff. The fashion-forward rule is simple—match volume with clarity. If the sleeve is dramatic, keep the neckline and hair clean. If the skirt carries the movement, let the top remain exact.

title: Mercedes Salazar in Bogotá: Jewelry with Joy, Magic and Colombian Soul
dek: Jewelry with joy, magic and Colombian soul — oversized earrings, woven raffia bags, and a Bogotá atelier working with 200+ artisans.
body:
Mercedes Salazar in Bogotá

In Bogotá, where polished design lives beside exuberant color, Mercedes Salazar creates the kind of accessories that turn getting dressed into a small celebration. Her world is playful, exquisitely handmade and unmistakably Colombian: oversized earrings flutter like tropical wings, raffia bags become sculptural companions, and tiny charms carry stories far beyond their scale.

A Fashion Stroll Through Bogotá

Begin in the city’s elegant north, where leafy streets, galleries and destination shopping set an urbane rhythm. The Mercedes Salazar boutique at Centro Comercial El Retiro makes a natural stop on a Bogotá style itinerary. It is less a place for anonymous basics than an invitation to choose the piece that will define the entire look.

For another expression of Colombia’s refined, color-conscious fashion identity, continue our Silvia Tcherassi in Cartagena fashion stroll. Together, the two houses reveal how Colombian design can move from Caribbean ease to Bogotá wit without losing its sense of place.

The Designer Behind the Magic

Bogotá-born Mercedes Salazar studied technical jewelry in Mexico before returning home to establish her namesake brand. What began with bold, handmade necklaces grew into a broader universe of earrings, bags, charms and objects for the home. Across those categories, her signature remains wonderfully clear: generous scale, saturated color, movement and a deep curiosity about materials.

The beauty is never separated from the hands that make it. The brand says its jewelry and accessories are made by Colombian jewelers and artisans, and that it collaborates with more than 200 artisans around the country to help keep ancestral techniques alive. In the Bogotá atelier, traditional jewelry craft meets a fantastical design language inspired by nature, art and the energy of the universe.

Pieces to Notice

Statement Earrings

Salazar’s earrings are the instant mood-lifters: birds, flowers, wings and celestial forms rendered with theatrical lightness. Look for pairs with movement and a strong silhouette. They frame the face beautifully in photographs and make even a crisp white shirt feel intentional.

Woven Raffia Bags

The bags are equally expressive. Current designs such as the Swan Basket, Shelly Bag, Cherry Mini Basket and Mini Jungle Bag turn natural fibers into collectible conversation pieces. The El Edén story is especially meaningful: the brand describes natural straw shaped by more than 200 artisan families and finished through traditional craft in its Bogotá atelier.

Charms and Amulets

For a subtler entry into the world, choose a single charm or amulet. These smaller pieces layer easily onto a travel wardrobe and feel personal without becoming precious. A playful bag charm is also an elegant way to refresh a favorite tote already in your closet.

“In Bogotá, joy is a serious style credential.”

How Jet Set LatAM Would Style It

Let one Mercedes Salazar piece lead. For Bogotá, we love architectural black trousers, a silk ivory blouse, a cropped jacket and vivid earrings. For Cartagena, pair a woven mini bag with a fluid linen dress and flat metallic sandals. At dinner, pull the hair back, keep the neckline clean and allow a sculptural pair of earrings to do the talking.

The most fashion-forward approach is contrast: exuberant jewelry against tailoring, a whimsical basket beside a minimal column dress, or a tropical motif worn in the city. It feels sophisticated because the styling gives the craftsmanship room to breathe.

A Souvenir with a Point of View

Mercedes Salazar offers more than a finishing touch. Her pieces hold the optimism of color, the intimacy of handwork and the wit of a designer who sees nature as an endless cabinet of curiosities. Choose the earring that makes you smile, the bag that starts a conversation or the charm that becomes your travel talisman.
